papers.title_in_file: Toward Quantum-Aware Machine Learning: Improved Prediction of Quantum Dissipative Dynamics via Complex Valued Neural Networks
papers.version_note: arXiv:2601.03964v2, dated 26 to 27 February 2026, with the Supporting Information appended (20 pages in the text layer).
papers.what_it_is: A numerical comparison of complex-valued and real-valued neural networks that forecast reduced density matrices of the spin-boson model and 4-, 7- and 8-site FMO complexes.

existing.note: Table I (p.7 of the file) gives 1.06e-04 for the CVNN and 2.09e-04 for the RVNN on the 4-site complex, a ratio of 1.97. The supporting-information seed runs (Table S4) give smaller ratios for two of three seeds, so the twofold figure is one run.
existing.value: The authors report that the 4-site FMO complex shows a twofold trace accuracy improvement for the CVNN over the RVNN.
quotes: The 4-site FMO complex (comprising the four prominent sites of the full 7-site system) already shows a twofold trace accuracy improvement for the CVNN over the RVNN.

existing.note: The abstract claim is made without a qualification, but the results state that on the spin-boson model the two loss trajectories are nearly identical and that the advantages grow with system size; the spin-boson comparison is mixed (CVNN better on diagonal MAE, RVNN better on real coherence MAE).
existing.value: The authors report in the abstract that on the spin-boson model and Fenna-Matthews-Olson variants complex-valued neural networks outperform real-valued ones in convergence speed, training stability and physical fidelity; in the results they state that for the spin-boson model the CVNN and RVNN show nearly identical loss trajectories and that the advantages increase with system size and coherence complexity.

assertions.value: The authors state that both the RVNN and the CVNN are fully connected sequence-to-sequence networks of five layers (one input layer, three hidden layers and one output layer); the RVNN uses real weights, biases and ReLU, the CVNN uses complex weights, biases and a complex ReLU (CReLU) that applies ReLU separately to the real and imaginary components, and the CVNN parameter count was capped at a level approximately equal to or below the RVNN's.
assertions.anchor: Results, PDF p.4
quotes: Both models adopt a fully connected sequence-to-sequence architecture consisting of ﬁve layers: one input layer, three hidden layers, and one output layer.
combined with a complex ReLU (CReLU) activation function that applies the ReLU operation separately to the real and imaginary components.
we capped the number of trainable parameters in the CVNN at a level approximately equal to or below that of the RVNN.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own architecture in Section IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that the RVNN treats the real and imaginary components of each off-diagonal element as separate real degrees of freedom, while the CVNN encodes the upper-triangular reduced density matrix directly as a complex vector, embedding each real diagonal entry as a + ia at the input and discarding that additive phase at the output.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, PDF p.2 to p.3
quotes: the real and imaginary components akl, bkl are treated as separate degrees of freedom
We encode the upper-triangular RDM directly as a complex vector
we embed them uniformly into C by mapping a → a + ia at the input; at the output, this additive phase is discarded to maintain Hermiticity.
assertions.reader_inference: The CVNN layer in Eq. 12 is a real block matrix with the structure [[Wr, -Wi], [Wi, Wr]] acting on the stacked real and imaginary parts, which is a weight-tied special case of the general real layer in Eq. 10. With ReLU applied channelwise in both models, the CVNN is a parameter-tied real network; the paper does not test whether the gain comes from the tying or from the complex arithmetic.

assertions.value: The authors state that the upper-triangular representation enforces Hermiticity by construction, the lower triangle being recovered by conjugation.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, PDF p.3
quotes: and enforces Hermiticity by construction (the lower triangle is recovered by conjugation).
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Section II.A as a property of the representation.
assertions.reader_inference: The representation is described for the density matrix in general, so Hermiticity of the output holds for both models by construction. A search of the text finds no Hermiticity measurement in the Results.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that the CVNN gives significantly improved trace conservation and Hermiticity.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, PDF p.1
quotes: physical ﬁdelity—including signiﬁcantly improved trace conservation and Hermiticity
assertions.reader_inference: The Results report trace MAE (Table I), negative-eigenvalue counts (Table II) and element MAE (Table III). No Hermiticity result and no significance test appears in the text.

assertions.value: The authors define a CVNN layer as fC(z) = σC(Wz + b) with complex weights W and complex bias b, and write the linear part in real block form so that the real and imaginary parts transform jointly.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, Eqs. 11 and 12, PDF p.3
quotes: A CVNN layer computes fC(z) = σC(Wz + b)
This structured block matrix represents true complex multiplication
form jointly rather than independently
assertions.certainty_reason: The layer is defined in Section II.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that no RVNN can generate such rotations in a single step, because real weights act independently on the real and imaginary channels.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, PDF p.3
quotes: No RVNN can generate such rotations in a single step, because real weights act independently on Re and Im channels
assertions.reader_inference: The RVNN layer in Eq. 10 uses a full real weight matrix on the stacked real and imaginary inputs, and Eq. 12 shows the complex multiplication is itself a real matrix of that kind. So a real layer can represent the rotation and scaling; the statement holds only if real weights act channel by channel, which Eq. 10 does not say.

assertions.value: The authors state that the standard practice in RVNNs of decoupling the real and imaginary components risks discarding or obscuring correlations encoded in the complex geometry of quantum states.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, PDF p.2
quotes: This bifurcation risks discarding or obscuring the critical correlations that are holistically encoded within the complex geometry of quantum states

assertions.value: The authors state that the RVNN weights use He (Kaiming) uniform initialisation with biases set to zero, and that the CVNN assigns the real and imaginary part of each weight a reduced variance so that the complex weight matches the real He variance only after the two channels are combined, with the real and imaginary biases set to zero.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, PDF p.3 to p.4
quotes: we initialize each weight using the He (Kaiming) uniform distribution
matching the real He initialization only after combining the two channels.
we set both the real and imaginary parts to zero

assertions.value: The authors state a composite loss L = α1L1 + α2L2 + α3L3 + α4L4 made of a mean squared error term, a trace-preservation penalty, a penalty on negative eigenvalues and a penalty keeping eigenvalues within the interval [0, 1], with weights α1 = α2 = 1.0, α3 = 2.0, and α4 = 3.0.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, Eqs. 19 to 24, PDF p.5
quotes: we employ a composite loss function of the form L = α1L1 + α2L2 + α3L3 + α4L4,
physically admissible density matrices require all eigenvalues to lie within the interval [0, 1].
In all simulations reported here, we use α1 = α2 = 1.0, α3 = 2.0, and α4 = 3.0.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV states the loss and its weights.
assertions.reader_inference: The trace and positivity results in Tables I and II come from models trained with penalties aimed at those same quantities, so they measure how well each model meets a penalised target, not an unprompted property.

assertions.value: The authors report that the spin-boson training data come from the QD3SET-1 database, 1000 simulations in total (500 trajectories for the symmetric case and 500 for the asymmetric case) computed with the HEOM formalism; only the symmetric case (500 trajectories) is used, 400 of which are chosen for training by farthest point sampling, and the remaining trajectories are reserved for out-of-sample testing.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, PDF p.5 to p.6
quotes: training data are obtained from the openly accessible QD3SET1 database
In total, Dsb comprises 1000 independent simulations, with 500 trajectories for the symmetric case and 500 for the asymmetric case.
For the SB model, we consider only the symmetric case, comprising 500 trajectories from Dsb.
we then select 400 trajectories for training via farthest point sampling, with the remaining trajectories reserved for out-of-sample testing.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV states the data and split.
assertions.reader_inference: The text does not say which trajectories the validation loss in Fig. 2 uses; the held-out 100 are called out-of-sample test data.

assertions.value: The authors report that the 7-site and 8-site FMO data come from QD3SET-1, describing excitation initiated at site 1 and site 6 for the 7-site complex with site 8 added for the 8-site system, with 500 simulations for each initial excitation scenario propagated by a trace-conserving local thermalizing Lindblad master equation; the 4-site FMO data are generated by the authors with the same framework and bath parameters as the 7-site complex, with excitation localized on site 1.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, PDF p.5 to p.6
quotes: These datasets describe excitation energy transfer dynamics initiated at site 1 and site 6 for the 7-site complex, with site 8 additionally included for the 8-site system.
yielding a total of 500 simulations for each initial excitation scenario.
The quantum dynamics are propagated using a trace-conserving local thermalizing Lindblad master equation (LTLME)

Since a 4-site FMO model is not available in the QD3SET-1 database, we generate the corresponding dataset independently using the same LTLME framework and bath parameters as employed for the 7-site FMO complex, with the dynamics initialized by an excitation localized on site 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV states the FMO data sources.

assertions.value: The authors report that each spin-boson trajectory spans a total duration of 20/∆ with a time step of dt = 0.05, that the FMO dynamics is restricted to a total time of 2 ps with a time step of 0.005 ps, and that the models predict the next time steps in one forward pass: 81 input time steps and 40 predicted steps for the SB model, and 81 input time steps and 80 predicted steps for the FMO complexes.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, PDF p.6 to p.7
quotes: each trajectory spans a total duration of 20/∆ with a time step of dt = 0.05.
the FMO dynamics is restricted to a total time of 2 ps with a time step of 0.005 ps.
for the SB model, each training sample consists of 81 input time steps, and the network is trained to predict the subsequent 40 time steps.
with the models trained to predict the next 80 time steps.
assertions.reader_inference: The Supporting Information states a propagation to t = 50 ps for the FMO data, against 2 ps here; the two statements are not reconciled in the text.

assertions.reader_inference: With five fully connected layers and each complex weight and bias counted as two real numbers, the SB, 4-site and 7-site CVNN counts and all four RVNN counts reproduce exactly (e.g. RVNN SB = (324*64+64) + 3*(64*64+64) + (64*160+160) = 43680), and the 8-site CVNN count is 10 higher than the printed 1367276. So the cap holds in real parameters, and the CVNN reaches it with narrower hidden layers.

assertions.value: The authors report from training and validation loss curves over the first 100 training epochs that the CVNN and RVNN show nearly identical loss trajectories for the SB model, that for the 4- and 7-site FMO prototypes the CVNN reduces both training and validation loss consistently faster, and that this is most pronounced for the 8-site complex.

the CVNN and RVNN show nearly identical loss trajectories
For the 4- and 7-site FMO prototypes, the CVNN achieves a consistently faster reduction in both training and validation loss compared to the RVNN.
This advantage is most pronounced for the largest, coherence-rich 8-site FMO complex
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison rests on plotted curves for the first 100 of 100000 epochs; no final loss value for either model is tabulated in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CVNN's accuracy advantage, especially in capturing populations and key coherences, grows systematically as the open quantum system increases in size and coherence.
assertions.anchor: Results, PDF p.8
quotes: Together, these results demonstrate that the CVNN’s accuracy advantage—especially in capturing populations and key coherences—grows systematically as the open quantum system increases in size and coherence.
assertions.reader_inference: The evidence is four systems, each with one set of bath parameters shown and one reported run in the main tables; system size, coherence structure and bath parameters change together, and no ablation separates them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the CVNN's learning efficiency scales with system size, directly correlating with the increasing number and dynamical importance of complex-valued off-diagonal RDM elements.
assertions.anchor: Results, PDF p.7

assertions.reader_inference: No measurement of the importance of off-diagonal elements is shown against the loss gap; the explanation is asserted from the system-size trend.
